content: Dr Pepper is a caramel-colored, carbonated soft drink that is distributed in North America by Cadbury Schweppes Americas Beverages (CSAB), a division of Cadbury Schweppes. The headquarters of CSAB is located in Plano, Texas, a suburb of Dallas. In certain U.S. territories, the distribution rights are controlled by the Coca-Cola Company. A no-calorie version, Diet Dr Pepper, is also available, along with various other flavors. The drink was first sold in Waco, Texas, in 1885 and was introduced nationally in the United States at the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition as a new type of cola. However, Dr Pepper is not classified as a root beer. The U.S. Patent Office recognizes December 1, 1885, as the first time Dr Pepper was served. The drink was initially tested by its creator, Charles Alderton, who offered it to store owner Wade Morrison. After repeated testing, Alderton introduced the drink to customers at Morrison's soda fountain, where it became popular and was referred to as Waco. Alderton eventually gave the formula to Morrison. There is a popular belief that the drink was named after Morrison's former employer in Texas, but the Dr Pepper company disputes this, suggesting instead that Morrison may have named it after Dr. Charles T. Pepper, a physician from Virginia, near whom Morrison once lived. Dr Pepper is not marketed as a cola, unlike Coca-Cola and Pepsi. Its flavor is said to be derived from a blend of soda fountain flavors popular at the time of its creation. The exact formula, which includes 23 ingredients, remains a closely guarded secret. There is a long-standing urban legend that Dr Pepper contains prune juice, but the manufacturer has consistently denied this claim. A Dr Pepper Museum exists in downtown Waco, housed in the Artesian Manufacturing and Bottling Company building, which was the first facility built specifically to bottle Dr Pepper. The museum opened to the public in 1991 and features exhibits, a working old-fashioned soda fountain, and a gift store. In the mid-to-late 1980s, Dr Pepper nearly became a Coca-Cola brand. The company faced financial difficulties in the early 1980s, leading to a private buyout by an investment group. Coca-Cola later attempted to acquire Dr Pepper, but the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) blocked the merger due to antitrust concerns. Around the same time, the same investment group acquired Seven Up from Philip Morris, forming Dr Pepper/Seven Up, Inc. (DPSU). This restructuring led to the relinquishment of international branding rights for Dr Pepper in some regions. In the United States, CSAB does not have a complete network of bottlers and distributors, so Dr Pepper is sometimes bottled under contract by Coca-Cola or Pepsi bottlers. Before the Cadbury Schweppes buyout, 30% of Dr Pepper/Seven Up products were produced and distributed by Pepsi bottlers, another 30% by Coca-Cola bottlers, and the remaining 40% by independent bottlers and the Dr Pepper/Seven Up Bottling Group. Today, Dr Pepper relies heavily on the Cadbury Schweppes Bottling Group (formerly the Dr Pepper/Seven Up Bottling Group) for bottling and distribution in over 30 states. Coca-Cola and Pepsi have largely ceased bottling and distributing CSAB products, favoring their in-house alternatives, though regional exceptions exist. In Canada and Poland, Cadbury-Schweppes has licensed distribution rights to PepsiCo. In other countries, such as Mexico, Germany, and France, Cadbury-Schweppes owns the trademark and distributes the product. In most other parts of the world, Coca-Cola owns the trademark and distributes Dr Pepper due to antitrust regulations that prevented Coca-Cola from acquiring global rights. Dr Pepper is also available in Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. In the 1980s, the U.S. soft drink industry, including Dr Pepper, transitioned from using sugar to high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS) due to rising sugar prices caused by price supports and import quotas. However, some bottling plants, such as the one in Dublin, Texas, continue to use sugar. Dublin Dr Pepper, known for its use of cane sugar, has expanded its distribution to most of Texas and online. Other bottlers using sugar include Temple Bottling Company in Texas and West Jefferson Dr Pepper in North Carolina. In 2007, Coca-Cola bottlers in the Dr Pepper Heartland began selling limited-edition 16-ounce cans of Dr Pepper made with cane sugar, featuring the Old Doc logo. The period after Dr in the name was removed in the 1950s for stylistic and legibility reasons. The redesign of the logo at the time made Dr. appear as Di:, leading to the decision to drop the period permanently. This change also helped to eliminate any medical connotations associated with the product. Dr Pepper has been featured in various advertising campaigns, including the famous Be a Pepper series, which referred to fans of the drink as Peppers and often included elaborate dance scenes. The drink has also appeared in numerous films, TV shows, and pop culture references, such as Forrest Gump, The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou, and Mission to Mars. It has been involved in cross-promotions with Marvel Comics movies and has been featured in video games like Pikmin 2. Dr Pepper has introduced several flavors over the years, including Diet Dr Pepper, Cherry Vanilla Dr Pepper, and Berries & Cream Dr Pepper. The UK version of Dr Pepper has a different taste, resembling Coca-Cola Cherry, and is made with sugar instead of HFCS. The brand has also expanded into other products, such as jelly beans and barbecue sauces. Numerous imitation products exist, often using Dr or Mr in their names, such as Mr. Pibb (now Pibb Xtra), Dr. Thunder, and Dr. Bob. These imitations are sold by various retailers and manufacturers. Dr Pepper has played a significant role in U.S. antitrust history. In 1995, the FTC blocked a merger between Coca-Cola and Dr Pepper, citing concerns about monopolization of the pepper flavor category. The drink has been classified as a pepper-flavored beverage rather than a cola in legal and economic analyses.
